title: Systematic review and meta-analysis
note: A review is a study whose participants are other studies, so it can be done well or badly in the same ways. Two questions run through all of it: was the process fixed before the results were known, and is the pooled number built from studies that belong together? An undescribed method is Unclear, not a failure.

items.question: Were the question and the eligibility rules set down before the search began, in a protocol or registration that can be checked?
items.why: When eligibility is settled after the findings are known, studies can be let in or kept out on the strength of their results, and the pooled answer is shaped by hand.
lookFor: a registration number or published protocol, with a date before the search
population, intervention, comparator and outcome defined up front
the primary outcome named in advance, and whether the paper still leads with it
changes from the protocol, and whether they are declared and explained

items.question: Was the search wide enough to find the evidence, covering more than one database and reaching beyond what is easy to retrieve?
items.why: A search confined to one database and to published reports in one language misses studies systematically rather than randomly, and the ones it misses are disproportionately those that found nothing.
lookFor: the databases searched, with the dates covered and the date of the last search
the full strategy for at least one database, terms included
trial registries, conference abstracts, reference lists and contact with investigators
restrictions by language, date or publication status

items.question: Did two or more people screen the records and extract the data independently, with a stated way of settling disagreements?
items.why: A lone reviewer makes quiet slips in both directions and nothing catches them, so those errors travel straight into the pooled estimate.
lookFor: independent screening at title, abstract and full-text stages
independent extraction, or one person extracting and another checking
how disagreements were resolved, and how often they arose
a flow diagram with the numbers kept and dropped at each stage

items.question: Was each included study appraised for how it was conducted, and does that appraisal feed into what the review concludes?
items.why: Pooling turns several weak studies into one precise-looking number, and when the studies share a flaw the summary reproduces it with a tighter interval around it.
lookFor: a named appraisal method, applied to every included study
judgements reported study by study, not just as an average score
an analysis restricted to the soundest studies
whether the conclusion changes once the weakest studies are set aside

items.question: Was the scatter between the individual study results examined and explained, rather than only reported as a statistic?
items.why: Widely differing results mean the studies were not estimating one common effect, so an average across them can describe something that exists in no single setting.
lookFor: a forest plot showing each study's estimate and interval
a measure of inconsistency, or a prediction interval
subgroup or meta-regression analyses, and whether they were planned beforehand
one large or outlying study carrying the result

items.question: Are the studies alike enough in population, intervention and outcome definition for a single combined number to mean anything?
items.why: Averaging studies that asked different questions produces a figure that answers none of them, and the narrow interval around it hides how mixed the ingredients were.
lookFor: how far the populations, doses, schedules and comparators differ
outcome definitions and time points pooled together
the model chosen, fixed or random effects, and the reason given
whether a description of the studies would have been the honest alternative

items.question: Did the review confront the possibility that completed studies were never published, or that the small ones report larger effects than the large ones?
items.why: Studies with disappointing results appear late, in smaller journals, or not at all, so a synthesis of what is easy to find tends to overstate benefit.
lookFor: a funnel plot or asymmetry test, with enough studies to make it meaningful
registered studies whose results never appeared
unpublished data or grey literature actually obtained
whether the smallest studies are the ones driving the pooled effect

items.question: Is the confidence the pooled estimate deserves stated, taking in the soundness, the consistency, the precision and the relevance of what went into it?
items.why: A summary estimate inherits the weaknesses of its inputs, and a review that reports the number without saying how much to trust it invites the reader to treat it as settled.
lookFor: a rating per outcome, with the reasons for each downgrade
a summary table covering the outcomes that matter, not only the positive ones
absolute effects given alongside the ratio
whether the conclusion is worded more confidently than the rating allows

items.question: Do the populations, interventions and comparators inside the review match the patients and the usual care you are deciding about?
items.why: A pooled estimate describes the mixture of settings that went into it, so when your patients or your comparator sit outside that mixture, the number need not carry over.
lookFor: where and when the included studies were done
the range of doses, schedules and comparators that were pooled
outcomes that matter to patients, rather than surrogates
whether any subgroup of the included studies resembles your patients

info.title: Funding & conflicts
info.prompt: Who funded the study, what role did the funder or sponsor have in the design, conduct, analysis and reporting, and what relevant conflicts of interest were declared?
info.why: Industry funding is not itself a risk of bias, and a trial paid for by a manufacturer is not wrong for that reason. What matters is what the sponsor was in a position to do, and what was declared, so record these as facts and let the methodological items above carry the judgement.

fields.label: Funder
fields.hint: Who paid: name the company, agency, charity or grant. Record "not stated" when no funding statement is given.

fields.label: Sponsor or funder role
fields.hint: What they did in design, conduct, data collection and custody, analysis, writing, and the decision to publish. A named funder with no role described is "unclear", not "none".

fields.label: Author conflicts declared
fields.hint: Payments, advisory or speaker roles, employment, stock or patents relevant to this intervention, and whether any declaration statement appears at all.

fields.label: Where this came from
fields.hint: Which document told you: the published abstract, the funding statement in the full text, the disclosure forms, or the registry record. Say if you only had one of them.
